extracted.intended_audience: students/readers learning undergraduate real analysis and elementary calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter material on limits, continuity, compactness, and maxima/minima including Bolzano and Weierstrass theorems, illustrative examples and geometric applications. Focuses on existence proofs, sequence methods, and elementary techniques for solving extremum problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass theorem on extreme values (closed interval)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x) is continuous on a closed interval a ≤ x ≤ b, then f(x) attains a largest and a smallest value on that interval (i.e., there exist points where the maximum M and minimum m are attained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch via nested closed subintervals: repeatedly bisect and select subinterval containing the greatest value to produce nested intervals whose intersection gives a point z with f(z)=M; contradiction argument using continuity shows no larger value exists. Existence of least value follows similarly or from greatest value of g(x)=M-f(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass theorem on extreme values (general compact set)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u = F(X) is any continuous real-valued function defined on a compact set S (in a metric/’distance’ space), then there exists an element of S at which F(X) attains its largest value, and one at which it attains its smallest value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization of the closed-interval result using the sequential-compactness definition of compactness: every sequence in S has a convergent subsequence with limit in S. The same nested-interval or subsequence argument applies in the abstract setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano's theorem (intermediate value/existence principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function on an interval assumes all intermediate values: if a continuous function takes values of opposite sign at two points, it has a zero between them. More generally, continuity guarantees existence of intermediate function values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly as an existence tool rather than a constructive method: examples include finding a line that bisects an area (define a continuous area-difference function and apply Bolzano), finding angles producing equal area pieces, and proving existence points in mechanics problems (train rod example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of compact set (sequential compactness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set S (with a notion of distance) is compact if from any sequence X1, X2, X3,... of elements of S one can always extract a subsequence that tends to some limit element X of S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: closed interval [a,b], closed rectangle, and the set of triangles whose vertices lie within/on a given circle are compact. The whole real line and open intervals like (0,1) are not compact (provide counterexample sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence-based definition of continuity (general spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function u = F(X) (X in S) is continuous at X if for every sequence Xn in S tending to X, the corresponding numbers F(Xn) tend to F(X). An equivalent (ε,δ) definition exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sequence formulation extends continuity from real-variable functions to functions on any metric-like set (e.g., triangles with a distance defined). It is used to generalize theorems like Weierstrass to abstract settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested intervals (interval bisection) method for existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To locate an extremum or root on a closed interval, iteratively divide the interval into two closed halves and select the half known (by comparison) to contain the desired value, producing a nested sequence of closed intervals whose intersection is the target point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the Weierstrass proof to find a point where the maximum is attained. The limit point of nested closed intervals contains the extremal point by continuity. This is an existence, not a constructive algorithm for exact location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs via continuity vs constructive methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Many theorems proved by continuity arguments show that an object with a desired property exists, but do not provide a definite procedure to construct it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the line bisecting two areas: Bolzano guarantees existence of angle producing simultaneous bisection, but no constructive method is given. Emphasize difference between mathematical existence proofs and explicit constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze (sandwich) technique for limits of sequences/functions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove convergence of a sequence an, find two sequences bn ≤ an ≤ cn for all n, where bn and cn converge to the same limit a; then an also converges to a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical use involves elementary inequalities to bound a complicated sequence between simpler sequences. The text leaves the formal proof to the reader and demonstrates with examples (e.g., estimating nth-root behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary rules for manipulating inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic operations with inequalities: (1) add same number to both sides, (2) multiply both sides by positive number preserves inequality, (3) multiply by -1 reverses inequality, (4) if a and b have same sign and a < b then 1/a > 1/b, (5) |a+b| ≤ |a| + |b| (triangle inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules are recalled because applications of the squeeze technique and many limit arguments rely on careful inequality manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of geometric sequence behavior q^n
rubrics_metrics.description: If q>1 then q^n → ∞; if q=1 then q^n =1; if |q|<1 then q^n → 0; if q<-1 then q^n alternates and has no limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch for q>1: write q=1+h and compare to nh to show divergence. For |q|<1 use monotone bounded sequence argument when 0<q<1 and absolute value trick for negative q. Exercise: rigorous proof for q<-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of nth roots: p^{1/n} → 1
rubrics_metrics.description: For any fixed positive number p, the sequence p^{1/n} (positive nth root) tends to 1 as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses inequalities by setting p^{1/n} = 1 + h_n (or reciprocal case) and bounding h_n (e.g., h_n < p/n) to show h_n→0. Also gives estimate for difference between p^{1/n} and 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of discontinuous functions as limits of continuous functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain discontinuous functions can be obtained as pointwise limits of sequences of continuous functions fn(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fn(x) = 1/(1+x^{2n}) tends to a piecewise function taking values 1, 1/2, 0 depending on |x|<1, |x|=1, |x|>1; other rational-function sequences approximate discontinuous functions. This shows limits of continuous functions need not be continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration methods and convergence for solving equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a sequence by an+1 = Phi(an) (iteration); if the sequence is monotone and bounded it converges, and its limit satisfies the fixed-point equation a = Phi(a), which can solve algebraic equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: iterative scheme an+1 = sqrt(1+an) gives a monotone increasing bounded sequence converging to positive root of x^2 = 1 + x. Iteration yields numeric approximations and existence proofs; monotonicity and boundedness are the usual convergence checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity verification via epsilon-delta or differentiability
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove continuity of a function at a point, verify the epsilon-delta condition; if a function is differentiable it is automatically continuous, which simplifies many proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstrates an explicit epsilon-delta style estimate for f(x)=1/(1+x^2) on a bounded interval and notes that in practice continuity proofs are often omitted when differentiability is established later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heron's theorem (reflection method for shortest path)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a line L and points P and Q on the same side of L, the point R on L minimizing PR + RQ is obtained by reflecting P across L to P' and taking intersection of P'Q with L; the minimizing path satisfies equal angles of incidence/reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via reflection: PR+RQ = P'R + RQ = P'Q at the minimizing point; triangle inequality shows any other point gives larger sum. Generalizes to multiple reflections (multiple mirrors) by successive reflections of Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremum characterizations yield geometric tangent properties (ellipse/hyperbola)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipse: locus p+q = constant (foci P,Q) and tangent at R has property that PR and RQ make equal angles with the tangent (follows from minimality of PR+RQ). Hyperbola: locus |p-q|=constant and tangent at R bisects angle between RP and RQ (follows from extremal difference property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classical tangent properties are derived by interpreting ellipse/hyperbola definitions as extremum problems and applying the reflection construction and extremal arguments; also discuss which branch is touched and special case of asymptote when P and Q equidistant from tangent line.
